title: Thermodynamics with thermodynamic variable first-passage time. I. From stochastic trajectories to nonlinear transport equations
abstract: The theoretical foundation of combining external nonequilibrium thermodynamics, the nonequilibrium statistical operator method, and stochastic first passage time thermodynamics are explored. It is shown that including a random lifetime of a metastable state in the generalized distribution function allows the first passage time to be considered as a fully - fledged macroscopic coordinate. A microscopic justification for this approach is provided, and a generalized thermodynamic potential is introduced. A procedure for closing the transport equations based on on thermodynamic consistency conditions is developed. It is shown that in the generalized Maxwell - Catteneo equation, the classical relaxation time is strictly replaced by the mean first passage time, which imparts internal macroscopic nonlinearity to the system. Using renewal theory, the exact mathematical structure of transport memory kernels for non-Markovian processes is derived. A qualitative comparative analysis of various approaches to the thermodynamic description of nonequilibrium phenomena is presented.
summary: This paper develops an advanced thermodynamic theory that treats the time taken to escape a metastable state (First-Passage Time) as a primary thermodynamic variable. It rigorously connects stochastic trajectory statistics to macroscopic transport equations by showing that fluctuation-dissipation theorems uniquely determine memory effects, thereby providing a nonlinear description of non-equilibrium dynamics.
main_problem: To develop a rigorous theoretical framework for nonequilibrium thermodynamics that incorporates the first-passage time (FPT) as an independent, macroscopic thermodynamic variable.
main_result: The mean FPT replaces classical relaxation times in transport equations, introducing inherent macroscopic nonlinearity. Furthermore, the memory kernel governing non-Markovian processes is uniquely determined by the microscopic statistics of state lifetimes via fluctuation-dissipation relations.
method: The authors combine Nonequilibrium Statistical Operator (NSO) methods with renewal theory and generalized thermodynamic potential constructions to bridge stochastic trajectory dynamics to macroscopic transport equations.
model_or_system: The study models metastable systems undergoing phase transitions, such as superheated liquid boiling or nucleation processes. The system's evolution is analyzed in a high-dimensional phase space ($\Gamma$) relative to an absorbing boundary ($\partial\Omega$).
key_observables: First-Passage Time ($	ext{T}_{	ext{FPT}}$), Generalized Thermodynamic Potential ($\Phi$), Macroscopic Memory Kernel ($K(t)$), and Entropy Production ($\sigma$).
important_parameters: The mean first passage time $\langle 	ext{T}_{	ext{fpt}} angle$ acts as a key macroscopic parameter, replacing the classical relaxation time $	au$. The system is analyzed near critical points where barrier deformation occurs.
main_assumptions: The central assumption is that FPT can be treated as a fully-fledged macroscopic coordinate. Consistency requires satisfying fluctuation-dissipation relations and assuming Bogolyubov's timescale separation.

paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical foundation (bridging EIT/NSO with FPT), deriving generalized potentials using stochastic methods, and finally enforcing thermodynamic consistency by showing that fluctuation-dissipation theorems uniquely determine the non-Markovian transport memory kernels.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general framework for understanding how microscopic stochastic dynamics (like crossing an energy barrier) dictates macroscopic transport properties in systems far from equilibrium, which is crucial for modeling complex processes like phase transitions or reaction kinetics.
